title: 1099-NEC vs. 1099-MISC: Which Form Should Your Startup File?
summary: 1099-NEC vs. 1099-MISC: Which Form Should Your Startup File?
body_markdown:
Your startup pays a designer, an office landlord, and a law firm. All three are vendors, but the payments may belong on different tax forms. The right starting point is what you paid for, followed by the recipient's tax classification and the payment method.


For a Delaware C-corp, these information returns are separate from Form 1120 and Delaware franchise tax filings.


## Use 1099-NEC for reportable nonemployee services


Form 1099-NEC generally reports compensation paid in your business to someone who is not an employee. Common startup examples include independent designers, consultants, and developers who are reportable U.S. payees.


For calendar-year 2026 payments, the general threshold is $2,000 or more per recipient. The threshold was $600 for 2025 payments. Backup withholding creates reporting obligations even below the ordinary threshold. If you pay an eligible designer $8,000 by bank transfer in 2026, report the full qualifying amount, not just the excess over $2,000.


## Use 1099-MISC for specified other payments


Form 1099-MISC covers categories such as rent, royalties, and certain other income. For 2026, the threshold rises to $2,000 for several categories, including rents, prizes, other income, and medical payments. Royalties generally retain a $10 threshold, while gross proceeds paid to attorneys generally retain a $600 threshold. Review the category-specific[IRS instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) .


For example, qualifying office rent paid to an individual landlord can belong in the rents box. A bonus paid for a contractor's services remains service compensation; calling it a prize does not change its purpose.


## Legal payments need an extra review


Fees for an attorney's services generally belong on 1099-NEC when reportable. Gross proceeds paid to an attorney in connection with legal services, such as certain settlement payments, can belong on 1099-MISC instead. The ordinary corporate-payee exemption does not remove these attorney reporting rules.


Before paying a settlement, have counsel and your tax preparer identify the recipients and reporting categories. One settlement can produce more than one reporting obligation.


## Check payee and payment-method exceptions


A W-9 helps establish whether a vendor is a sole proprietor, partnership, or corporation for federal tax purposes. An LLC can have different tax classifications. Foreign vendors need a separate documentation and withholding review.


Payments settled by payment cards or qualifying third-party networks generally fall under 1099-K reporting by the settlement entity and are excluded from your NEC or MISC reporting. Do not assume every software-mediated ACH payment qualifies. See the[IRS payment reporting guidance](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/reporting-payments-to-independent-contractors) .


## Keep deadlines and responsibilities separate


For 2026 compensation, 1099-NEC is generally due to recipients and the IRS on February 1, 2027. MISC recipient and IRS deadlines differ by copy, box, and filing method. Use the[general instructions](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p1099) to calendar the exact dates, including weekend and holiday adjustments.


Give each vendor review five fields: annual amount, payment purpose, tax classification, payment method, and filing conclusion. That simple record lets your accounting team explain both the forms issued and the payments properly excluded.
